title: LPIC-1 Exam 101 (101-500) practice exam

domains.name: Devices, Linux Filesystems, Filesystem Hierarchy Standard

note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public LPIC-1 Exam 101 (101-500) objectives, v5.0. Not real exam questions. Practice on your own lab machines (WSL, a VM or a cloud sandbox), never on production systems you don't manage. 104.4 was removed in v5.0; two items tagged 104.4 cover du and df only.

q.q: A new PCIe network card is installed, but no interface for it appears in `ip link`. You want to know whether the kernel sees the card at all and which driver, if any, is bound to it. Which command is the best first step?
o: lspci -k
Right. Lists PCI devices and, with -k, the kernel driver in use and the modules that could drive each one. A card with no "Kernel driver in use" line points to a missing or unloaded driver.
lsusb -t -v
Shows only USB devices and their tree. A PCIe card never appears there.
lsmod | grep -i net
Lists loaded modules, but not which hardware they are bound to, so it will not tell you whether the card was detected.
cat /proc/ioports
Shows I/O port ranges claimed by drivers. It is not the way to find out which device has no driver.

q.q: A USB 3 disk is slow. You need to see the USB bus topology as a tree, with the driver bound to each device and the speed each port negotiated (5000M or 480M). Which command shows that?
o: lspci -t
This draws the PCI bus as a tree. A USB disk hangs off a USB bus, which this does not list.
lsusb -t
Right. The -t option prints the USB devices as a tree by bus and port, with the driver and the speed of each, so a USB 3 disk that fell back to 480M stands out.
lsusb -d 0781:
-d only filters the list to one vendor and product ID. It does not draw the tree or show port speeds.
lsblk -t
-t shows I/O topology of block devices, such as sector sizes, not the USB ports they use.

q.q: You must stop the `pcspkr` module from loading at every boot, even if another module lists it as a dependency or udev tries to autoload it. Which line in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ does this most reliably?
o: blacklist pcspkr
A blacklist stops only alias-based autoloading by udev. A dependency pull or a manual modprobe still loads the module.
options pcspkr disable=1 quiet=1
options passes parameters to a module when it loads. It does not stop the load, and this module has no such parameter.
alias pcspkr off
An alias line maps a name to a module. The name off is not a module, so this does not block anything useful.
install pcspkr /bin/false
Right. An install line replaces the normal load action with a command that fails, so the module cannot be loaded, even as a dependency.

q.q: After you edit a file in /etc/udev/rules.d/, which command makes udev read the new rules without a reboot?
o: udevadm info --export-db
This only prints the current udev database. It reloads nothing.
systemctl daemon-reload --user
Reloads systemd unit files, not udev rules.
udevadm control --reload
Right. This tells the running udev daemon to re-read its rules files. Use udevadm trigger afterward to re-apply them to devices already present.
modprobe --reload-rules --all
modprobe has no such option. It loads and unloads kernel modules.

q.q: A USB backup disk with serial number ABC123 should always get the extra name /dev/backup, whatever sdX letter it receives. Which udev rule does this?
o: SUBSYSTEM=="block", ENV{ID_SERIAL_SHORT}=="ABC123", NAME="backup"
Udev cannot rename block devices (NAME is ignored for them). Extra names are made with SYMLINK.
SUBSYSTEM="block", ENV{ID_SERIAL_SHORT}="ABC123", SYMLINK="backup"
A single = assigns a value instead of testing it. In a match key it is a syntax error, so no rule would match.
SUBSYSTEM=="block", ENV{ID_SERIAL_SHORT}=="ABC123", SYMLINK+="backup"
Right. == matches the device and SYMLINK+= adds a link next to the kernel name. The rule fires whenever this disk appears.
ACTION=="remove", ENV{ID_SERIAL_SHORT}=="ABC123", SYMLINK+="backup"
This only fires when the disk is removed, when it is too late to create a usable link.

q.q: Which TWO of the following are virtual filesystems that the kernel generates in memory and that hold no ordinary data on disk? (Choose two.)
o: /var/log
Holds log files stored on disk.
/proc
Right. It shows live process and kernel information, and the files are created as you read them.
/home
Holds user files on disk.
/boot
Holds the kernel, the initramfs and boot loader files on a normal disk partition.
/sys
Right. sysfs exposes devices, drivers and kernel settings as a tree of attributes built by the kernel.

q.q: On a UEFI system, where does firmware look first to find the boot loader program?
o: In the first 440 bytes of the first sector of the disk, the MBR
That is how legacy BIOS boots. UEFI does not need that code.
In the /boot/grub/menu.lst file
That is an old GRUB Legacy text file. Firmware does not read files by path from the root filesystem.
In the initramfs image of the newest kernel
The initramfs is loaded after the boot loader, not before it.
In the EFI System Partition, a small FAT partition
Right. UEFI reads the boot entries in NVRAM and runs the .efi file on the ESP, for example grubx64.efi. No boot code is needed in the first sector.

q.q: What is the main job of the initramfs during boot?
o: To check the integrity of all files in /etc before the services start
The initramfs does not scan /etc files. Integrity tools such as AIDE do that later.
To provide the drivers needed to mount the real root filesystem
Right. The boot loader loads it into memory beside the kernel. It can unlock encrypted disks, assemble RAID or LVM, then hand control to the real root.
To store the kernel boot parameters between reboots
Boot parameters come from the boot loader configuration. The initramfs does not keep them.
To replace the BIOS or UEFI firmware at startup
The firmware runs before anything on disk. The initramfs is only used after the kernel starts.

q.q: An admin must see the log messages from the current boot only, on a system that uses systemd-journald with persistent storage. Which command does this?
o: journalctl -b
Right. The -b option limits output to the current boot. Add -b -1 for the previous boot.
journalctl --since boot-1
There is no such time keyword. The command would reject it.
dmesg --previous
dmesg shows only the kernel ring buffer of the current boot. It has no --previous option for older boots.
cat /var/log/boot
A plain /var/log/boot file is not part of a normal systemd system, and it would not hold the journal.

q.q: You are at the GRUB 2 menu and want to boot once into single-user (rescue) mode without changing any file. What is the quickest way?
o: Edit /etc/default/grub on the running system, run update-grub and reboot
That changes the saved default for every later boot, not just one.
Press e on the entry, append systemd.unit=rescue.target, boot with Ctrl+x
Right. Edits made in the menu apply to that one boot only. The kernel passes systemd.unit= to systemd, which starts rescue.target.
Press c and run `init 1` at the GRUB command line, then press Enter
The GRUB prompt is not a shell. It has no init command and cannot switch runlevels.
Press F2 to open the firmware setup and choose rescue
Firmware setup chooses boot devices. It has no option to select a Linux rescue mode.

q.q: On a server that still uses the SysV init system, which file lists the default runlevel to enter after boot?
o: /etc/default/grub
This file sets GRUB menu options, not the runlevel that init enters.
/etc/runlevel.conf
No such file exists in standard SysV init.
/etc/inittab
Right. The line `id:3:initdefault:` sets the default runlevel on SysV init systems.
/proc/cmdline
This shows what was passed to the running kernel. It cannot be edited to set a default.

q.q: A Linux machine hangs right after the kernel starts, with a black screen. You want the kernel to print all messages to the console to find the cause. Which kernel parameter removes the quiet and splash behavior?
o: Add `nomodeset=off` to the line and keep `quiet` in place
quiet still hides most messages, and nomodeset=off is not a valid switch.
Add `init=/bin/sh` only
This starts a shell as the first process instead of init, which skips the normal startup. It does not turn on more messages.
Add `ro` to the command line
ro mounts root read-only at boot, which is normal. It does not change the amount of messages.
Remove `quiet` and `splash` from the kernel line for one boot
Right. quiet suppresses most kernel messages and splash shows a graphic. Removing them shows the boot text on the console.

q.q: Which TWO items does the boot loader place into memory before it hands control to the kernel? (Choose two.)
o: The /etc/fstab file
The mounts in this file are read by systemd long after the loader is finished.
The kernel image
Right. The loader reads the kernel file from /boot and loads it into RAM.
The initramfs image
Right. It is loaded beside the kernel so the kernel can reach the real root filesystem.
The login program
The login program is started by a service once the system is up.
The systemd unit files
systemd reads these after the kernel has started, when it begins as PID 1.

q.q: A server must boot to a text-only multi-user target by default. What is the correct command to set that permanently on a systemd system?
o: systemctl set-default multi-user.target
Right. This changes the default.target symlink, so the target is used on every boot.
systemctl isolate multi-user.target --job-mode=replace
isolate switches the target right now, but the change is not kept for the next boot.
systemctl enable multi-user.target --now
enable only adds a unit to a target's wants. It does not change the default target.
telinit 3
telinit changes the runlevel now only. The change is not saved by systemd.

q.q: An administrator wants to move a running systemd server to rescue mode now without rebooting. Which command does it?
o: systemctl set-default rescue.target
That only changes the default for the next boot. The current session stays as it is.
systemctl mask rescue.target --runtime
Masking makes a unit impossible to start. It does the opposite of what you want.
systemctl reload-or-restart rescue.target
reload asks a service to re-read its settings. A target does not do that.
systemctl isolate rescue.target
Right. isolate starts the named target and stops units that it does not need, so only a basic system with a root shell remains.

q.q: You must reboot a server in 20 minutes and show every logged-in user a custom message. Which command does this in one step?
o: shutdown -r +20 "Rebooting for patches"
Right. -r means reboot, +20 is minutes from now, and the text is sent to every logged-in terminal. shutdown -c cancels it.
shutdown -h +20 "Rebooting for patches"
-h halts the system, so it would power off and not come back up.
reboot -f +20 "Rebooting for patches"
reboot takes no delay argument, so this fails and does not schedule anything.
wall -r 20 "Rebooting for patches"
wall only sends a message to users. It does not reboot anything and has no -r option.

q.q: A scheduled shutdown was started with `shutdown -h +60` by mistake. Which command cancels it?
o: shutdown -k +60
-k only sends warnings without shutting down. It does not cancel a shutdown that is already pending.
shutdown -c
Right. The -c option cancels a pending shutdown that is waiting for its timer.
kill -9 1 (the init process)
This tries to kill the init process, which the kernel protects, and it is dangerous.
halt --cancel
halt has no such option.

q.q: Which pair correctly maps a SysV runlevel to its systemd target on most distributions?
o: Runlevel 1 and graphical.target (full desktop)
Runlevel 1 is single-user maintenance, which matches rescue.target. graphical.target is runlevel 5.
Runlevel 5 and rescue.target
Runlevel 5 is the graphical system and matches graphical.target.
Runlevel 3 with multi-user.target
Right. Runlevel 3 is a text-mode multi-user system with networking, which matches multi-user.target.
Runlevel 0 and reboot.target
Runlevel 0 matches poweroff.target. Runlevel 6 matches reboot.target.

q.q: A server will not finish booting because a unit in a mounted data volume failed. At the GRUB menu you want a minimal environment with only essential services and a root prompt, where the root filesystem is mounted read-only. Which kernel argument is closest to that?
o: systemd.unit=graphical.target
This starts the full graphical environment, which is the opposite of minimal.
systemd.unit=emergency.target
Right. emergency.target starts a root shell after mounting only the root filesystem, read-only, with almost no services. It is the most minimal mode.
systemd.unit=poweroff.target
This powers the machine off right after boot.
systemd.unit=network-online.target
This only marks that the network is up. It is not a mode that gives you a shell.

q.q: A UEFI machine has a GPT disk. Which partition is required so that the firmware can start the boot loader?
o: An EFI System Partition, FAT32, mounted at /boot/efi
Right. UEFI firmware reads .efi programs from the ESP, and the specification requires a FAT filesystem on it.
A BIOS boot partition of 1 MiB with no filesystem on it
That is used when GRUB boots a GPT disk on a legacy BIOS system, not on UEFI.
A swap partition of at least the size of RAM
Swap is for virtual memory and has no role in booting. Booting also works with no swap.
A separate /usr partition formatted with the ext4 filesystem
/usr can be separate but is not needed to start the boot loader.

q.q: Which is the best reason to place /var on its own partition on a busy mail and log server?
o: The kernel then loads faster because /var is read first
The kernel is not read from /var, so this does nothing for boot time.
It lets /var use a different kernel from the root filesystem
There is only one running kernel. Partitions do not choose a kernel.
Runaway logs or spool files cannot fill the root filesystem
Right. A separate /var limits the damage when logs, spool or caches grow without control. The system under / keeps working.
It removes the need for any swap space
Swap is a separate matter. A separate /var has no effect on whether swap is needed.

q.q: On a system that uses LVM for everything except /boot, why must /boot remain outside LVM on many older setups?
o: LVM cannot store files larger than 100 MB
LVM does not limit file sizes. The filesystem on top does, and ext4 and XFS handle files far larger.
The kernel refuses to start from a logical volume that has snapshots
Snapshots are not the reason. The issue is whether the loader can read the volume.
/boot has to be mounted by the user at login time
/boot is mounted at boot from /etc/fstab. It is not mounted by users.
The boot loader reads the kernel before LVM is active, and some loaders cannot read LVM
Right. Older loaders and some configurations cannot activate volume groups. A plain partition avoids that problem.

q.q: A server has no free partition, but it needs 4 GB of swap now. Which sequence creates and turns on a swap file, with safe permissions?
o: touch /swapfile, then swapon /swapfile
An empty file has no size and no swap signature, so swapon refuses it.
mkfs.ext4 /swapfile, then mount /swapfile /swap
Swap is not a mounted filesystem. It needs mkswap and swapon, and an ext4 filesystem on the file would not be swap.
mkswap /swapfile, then swapon /swapfile, with no step to create the file
mkswap cannot prepare a file that does not exist yet. The file must be created at the right size first.
fallocate -l 4G /swapfile, chmod 600 /swapfile, mkswap /swapfile, swapon /swapfile
Right. The file is created at full size, locked to root, given a swap signature by mkswap and then enabled. An /etc/fstab line would keep it after a reboot.

q.q: After editing /etc/default/grub on a Debian-based system, which command rebuilds the GRUB configuration file?
o: grub-install /dev/sda
This writes the boot loader to the disk. It does not regenerate the menu file from your changes.
vi /boot/grub/grub.cfg
grub.cfg is generated and your manual edits are lost the next time it is regenerated.
update-grub
Right. On Debian and Ubuntu this wrapper runs grub-mkconfig and writes /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
dpkg-reconfigure grub-menu
No package or command with this name regenerates the configuration.

q.q: On a RHEL-family system with BIOS firmware, which command writes the GRUB 2 boot code to the MBR of the first disk?
o: grub2-install /dev/sda
Right. The command copies the GRUB 2 stage files to the disk. On BIOS it writes to the MBR.
grub2-mkconfig -o /dev/sda
-o names the output file for the generated configuration. Pointing it at a disk device would overwrite data and never install the loader.
dd if=/boot/grub2/grub.cfg of=/dev/sda
This would write text over the disk start and corrupt it.
fdisk --install-grub /dev/sda
fdisk edits partition tables. It has no option to install a loader.

q.q: In the GRUB 2 interactive prompt (not rescue) you see `grub>` after a failed boot. Which pair of commands sets the root and loads a kernel by hand?
o: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt, then chroot /mnt
The GRUB prompt has no mount or chroot. Those are shell commands.
set root, then linux and initrd lines, then boot
Right. This tells GRUB which partition to read, loads the kernel with its root parameter and the initramfs, and then starts it.
init 3 then startx
init and startx are not GRUB commands. They run only after Linux has started.
systemctl start boot.target and wait for it
systemd is not running at the GRUB prompt, so systemctl does not exist there.

q.q: Which file contains the setting GRUB_TIMEOUT that sets how long the menu is shown at boot?
o: /boot/grub/device.map
This maps GRUB names to device names. It has no timeout setting.
/etc/grub.d/00_header
This is a script that generates parts of the file. Normal settings go in /etc/default/grub, not in the script.
/etc/default/grub
Right. The values here feed the grub-mkconfig script. Regenerate the config after changing them.
/etc/fstab
fstab holds the filesystems to mount, not the boot menu settings.

q.q: Which command shows the shared libraries an executable needs and where each one was found?
o: ldd /usr/bin/ssh
Right. ldd prints each needed library and the path where the dynamic linker finds it, or "not found" if it is missing.
ldconfig -r /usr/bin/ssh
ldconfig rebuilds the library cache. It does not report the needs of a program.
lsmod | grep ssh
lsmod lists kernel modules. Program libraries are not kernel modules.
file /usr/bin/ssh
file only shows the type of the file, not its library list.

q.q: You added a new directory /opt/acme/lib that holds libraries, and put the path in a file in /etc/ld.so.conf.d/. The program still cannot find them. What is the next step?
o: Reboot the machine twice
A reboot would eventually rebuild it, but it is not required. ldconfig does it right away.
Run ldconfig as root
Right. The dynamic linker uses the cache /etc/ld.so.cache. ldconfig reads the .conf files and updates it.
Set the sticky bit on the new directory
The sticky bit controls who may delete files in a directory. It does not affect library search.
Run ldd on the new directory
ldd checks programs, not directories, and does not change the cache.

q.q: Which command lists the files that the installed package `openssh-server` put on a Debian system?
o: dpkg -S openssh-server
-S searches for which package owns a file path. It does not list a package's files.
apt-cache depends openssh-server
This shows the dependencies of the package, not its files.
dpkg --print-avail openssh-server
-p prints the package record, such as version, size and description. It does not list the files.
dpkg -L openssh-server
Right. -L lists files owned by an installed package.

q.q: You have a file /usr/sbin/sshd and want to learn which installed Debian package owns it. Which command answers that?
o: dpkg --listfiles /usr/sbin/sshd
This option (--listfiles, same as -L) expects a package name, not a path, so it would fail here.
dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd
Right. -S looks up a path in the package database and prints the owning package.
apt-get source /usr/sbin/sshd
This downloads source code for a package name. A file path is not a package name.
apt-file update
This refreshes a database for apt-file. It does not answer the question.

q.q: The command `dpkg -i foo.deb` stops with an error that a dependency is missing. Which command, run next, will fetch and install the missing packages and finish the job?
o: dpkg --purge --force-depends foo
Purging removes the package. It does not fix the missing dependency.
apt-get autoremove --purge
autoremove deletes packages that are no longer needed. It installs nothing.
apt-get install -f
Right. -f (fix-broken) pulls in the missing dependencies from the repositories and finishes the configuration.
dpkg-reconfigure foo
This reruns the configuration questions of an installed package. It does not install dependencies.

q.q: Which command removes a Debian package and also deletes its system-wide configuration files in /etc?
o: apt-get purge nginx
Right. purge removes the program files and the configuration files that the package placed under /etc.
apt-get remove nginx
remove deletes the program files but keeps the configuration files, so a later reinstall can reuse them.
apt-get clean
clean empties the cache of downloaded .deb files. It does not remove installed packages.
dpkg -r --keep-conf nginx
There is no such option. dpkg -r also leaves the configuration files.

q.q: Which file, together with the files in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/, tells APT which repositories to use?
o: /etc/apt/apt.conf
This holds APT settings such as proxy options, not the repository list.
/var/lib/dpkg/status
This records the installed packages. It does not name repositories.
/etc/dpkg/dpkg.cfg
This holds dpkg defaults, not repository addresses.
/etc/apt/sources.list
Right. Each line gives the type (deb or deb-src), the URL, the release name and the components.

q.q: After adding a new repository line, you run `apt-get install foo` and APT says it cannot find the package. What is the most likely missing step?
o: Run apt-get update to refresh the package lists
Right. APT searches its local package lists. A new repository is unknown until update downloads its lists.
Run apt-get upgrade to install all new versions
upgrade installs updates for installed packages. It does not refresh the lists first, and it would not change what is found.
Run dpkg --configure -a
This finishes the setup of packages that were left half-installed. It does not read new repositories.
Run apt-cache clean
There is no such sub-command, and nothing like it would add the new package.

q.q: Which command shows version, size, dependencies and description of a package that is available in the repositories but NOT installed?
o: dpkg -s nginx
-s reads the dpkg status database, which only has installed (or removed but configured) packages.
dpkg -L nginx-common
-L lists the installed files, so it fails for a package that is not installed.
apt-get check nginx-core
check looks for broken dependencies on the system. It does not describe a given package.
apt-cache show nginx
Right. It reads from the package lists, so it works for packages that are not installed.

q.q: You need to know which RPM package installed the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Which command tells you?
o: rpm -ql -v /etc/ssh/sshd_config
-ql lists the files of a package. It needs a package name, not a path.
rpm -qa --last /etc/ssh/sshd_config
-qa lists all installed packages, and a path is not a valid filter for it.
rpm -qf /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Right. -q queries, and -f finds the package that owns the file.
yum provides sshd
This looks for packages that provide a name, which is not the same as the owner of one installed file.

q.q: Which command checks whether the installed files of package `httpd` differ from the package's original size, mode, checksum or owner?
o: rpm -K -v httpd
-K checks the signature and digest of a package file, not the installed files.
rpm -V httpd
Right. -V verifies each file against the RPM database and prints a code for every property that changed.
rpm -e httpd --nodeps
-e erases the package. It does not check anything.
rpm -qi -v httpd
-qi shows general information about the package. It does not compare the files.

q.q: You downloaded foo-1.2.rpm and want to look at its file list without installing it. Which command does that?
o: rpm -ql foo --verbose
-ql queries the database of installed packages, so the package must already be installed.
rpm -Uvh foo-1.2.rpm
This installs or upgrades the package, so it changes the system.
rpm --rebuilddb --verbose
This rebuilds the RPM database. It does not show a package file's list.
rpm -qpl foo-1.2.rpm
Right. -p reads the package file instead of the database, and -l lists its files.

q.q: On a system that uses dnf, how do you find which package could supply a missing file, for example /usr/bin/dig, even if that package is not installed?
o: rpm -qf /usr/bin/dig
rpm -qf only knows about files that are already installed, so a missing file gives no answer.
dnf list installed /usr/bin/dig
list shows packages by name. A path is not a package name.
dnf provides /usr/bin/dig
Right. dnf searches the repository metadata for packages that supply the given file.
dnf clean all
This deletes cached data. It does not search for anything.

q.q: Which setting in a file under /etc/yum.repos.d/ tells dnf or yum to verify the signature of packages from that repository?
o: gpgcheck=1
Right. With the value 1, packages are checked against the GPG key given in gpgkey=, and unsigned or altered packages are refused.
enabled=1
enabled switches the repository on or off. It does not control signature checks.
baseurl=https://repo.example.org/
baseurl only gives the address of the repository.
skip_if_unavailable=0
This sets whether dnf fails when the repository is unreachable. It has no connection to signatures.

q.q: An RPM-based server has a package installed with a known bug and you must go back to the older version available in the repository. Which command is the best fit?
o: rpm -e --nodeps httpd
This removes the package and ignores dependencies, which can break the system, and installs nothing.
dnf downgrade httpd
Right. dnf finds the previous version in the enabled repositories and swaps it in, handling dependencies.
dnf upgrade --downgrade httpd
This option does not exist.
rpm --rollback httpd
RPM has no rollback option.

q.q: Which command lists the repositories that dnf currently has enabled on this system?
o: dnf list available
This lists packages that can be installed, not repositories.
dnf repolist
Right. With no extra options it shows enabled repositories and the number of packages in each.
rpm -qa --repos
This option does not exist in rpm.
dnf history
This shows past transactions such as installs and removals.

q.q: A VM was cloned, and the clone and its original now get the same DHCP lease because their DHCP clients send the same machine identity. Which file holds the unique ID that should be regenerated on the clone?
o: /etc/hostname
This only holds the name of the machine, and it is not used as the unique ID.
/etc/fstab
This lists the filesystems to mount. It has no machine identity.
/etc/machine-id
Right. systemd and some DHCP clients use this ID. After cloning, empty it and regenerate it so each machine has its own value.
/etc/resolv.conf
This lists DNS servers and has no unique ID.

q.q: A KVM host must freeze guest filesystems for a clean snapshot and read each guest's IP address without logging in. Which software must run inside the guest for this?
o: libvirtd
This is the management daemon on the host. It runs outside the guest and needs an agent in the guest to ask about its inside.
cloud-init
It configures an instance at first boot. It does not stay connected to the host to freeze disks or report addresses.
systemd-udevd
It handles device events in the guest. It has no channel to the hypervisor.
qemu-guest-agent
Right. The agent talks to the host over a virtio channel. It can freeze and thaw filesystems, report addresses and shut the guest down cleanly.

q.q: A cloud image boots with no password set. Which tool typically reads the provider's metadata at first boot to set the hostname, create users and add SSH keys?
o: cloud-init
Right. It reads data from the cloud provider on first boot and applies it, so one image can be used for many instances.
udevadm trigger
This manages and queries the device manager. It does not set up users from provider data.
anacron daemon
This runs periodic jobs that were missed while the machine was off.
lsblk
This lists block devices. It configures nothing.

q.q: You run `export LANG=C` in a shell, then start a script from that shell. Which statement is true?
o: Only the current shell sees LANG=C, and child processes still get the old value
That is what happens without export. Exporting is what passes a variable to children.
Every other terminal window now sees LANG=C as well
Environment variables are per process. Other terminals have their own copies.
The script and its child commands see LANG=C, and none of them changes the parent shell
Right. export marks the variable so it is copied into the environment of child processes. Children cannot change the parent's variables.
LANG=C is saved in /etc/environment for next login
A shell export is temporary and writes no file.

q.q: A user logs in on a text console and expects their alias definitions in ~/.bashrc to work, but they are not defined. The user's ~/.bash_profile exists and has no reference to ~/.bashrc. What is the cause?
o: Aliases are only allowed in /etc/profile
Users can define aliases in their own files. The system file is not the only place.
Bash ignores ~/.bashrc whenever the user's login shell is /bin/bash
Bash does read it, but only in interactive non-login shells or when it is sourced.
The alias command must be run by root
Any user can define aliases for their own shell.
A login shell reads ~/.bash_profile, not ~/.bashrc, unless the profile sources it
Right. Bash reads .bashrc only for interactive non-login shells. Many distributions add `source ~/.bashrc` to the profile for this reason.

q.q: Which command shows how bash would interpret the word `ll`, for example as an alias, a function, a builtin or a file?
o: type ll
Right. type reports the kind of command and where it comes from. It sees aliases, functions and builtins, which which does not always show.
whereis ll
whereis looks for binaries, manual pages and sources in standard places. It cannot see shell aliases.
file ll
file inspects the content of a file named ll. It does not look at how the shell resolves the word.
locate ll
locate searches a file name database. It does not resolve commands.

q.q: What does the command `echo "Today is $(date +%A)"` print on a Tuesday?
o: Today is $(date +%A)
This is what single quotes would produce. Double quotes do not stop $( ) from running.
Today is Tuesday
Right. Double quotes still allow command substitution, so $(date +%A) is replaced by the output of date, which is the day name.
Today is date +%A
The shell runs the command inside $( ) and puts in its output, not the text of the command.
Today is
The command is run, and its output is not empty.

q.q: Which command repeats the last command you typed, but with sudo in front of it, in bash?
o: sudo ^^
^^ is not a history expansion. It would be passed as text to sudo.
sudo !!
Right. !! is replaced by the previous command line. The shell shows the expanded line and runs it.
sudo $(history 1)
history 1 prints a line number before the command, so sudo would try to run the number as a command.
sudo !$
!$ is only the last argument of the previous command, not the whole line.

q.q: Which line removes variable `TMPDIR` so that it no longer exists in the current shell?
o: TMPDIR=
This sets the variable to an empty string. It still exists, though it is empty.
export -n TMPDIR=
export -n removes only the export flag. The variable remains in the shell, and the trailing = sets it empty.
rm TMPDIR
rm deletes files. It does not remove shell variables.
unset TMPDIR
Right. unset removes the variable and, if it was exported, removes it from the environment of later child processes too.

q.q: You run `man -k partition` and get a list. What did the command do?
o: It searched page names and descriptions for the word partition
Right. -k is the same as apropos. It lists matching pages so you can then open the right one.
It displayed the full text of every manual page that contains partition
-k lists only name and description lines. It does not print the pages.
It killed every process whose name contains the word partition
-k in man has nothing to do with processes.
It opened the manual page for a command named partition, if one exists
That would be `man partition`. With -k the argument is a keyword to search for.

q.q: A script works in your terminal, but `env -i ./job.sh` fails with `node: command not found`. Node lives in /opt/node/bin, which your login profile adds to PATH. What does this show, and what is a good fix?
o: env -i installs missing programs, so run it again until node is found
env only changes the environment of a command. It never installs anything.
The script needs chmod 777, because env -i drops file permissions
Permissions are stored on the file and env does not change them. The error says not found, not denied.
env -i clears the environment, so the PATH your profile built is gone. Set PATH inside the script or call /opt/node/bin/node by its full path
Right. env -i starts the script with an empty environment, so only the shell's built-in default PATH is used, and that default does not list /opt/node/bin.
Node can only be found when it is started from a login shell, so use `su -l`
Node is an ordinary program, and any shell finds it if PATH lists /opt/node/bin. A login shell only helps because the profile sets that PATH.

q.q: A script prints `10` for `echo $((3 + 7))`. Which feature of bash does this use?
o: Command substitution
Command substitution uses $( ) with a command inside, and it would try to run the text 3 + 7 as a command.
Brace expansion
Brace expansion uses { } to make lists such as {a,b,c}.
Tilde expansion
Tilde expansion changes ~ into a home directory.
Arithmetic expansion
Right. $(( )) evaluates the whole number expression and the result replaces it in the line.

q.q: Which TWO files does bash read when it starts as an interactive login shell? (Choose two.)
o: /etc/fstab
This lists filesystems to mount and has nothing to do with the shell.
~/.inputrc
This configures the readline library, such as key bindings, and is not a startup script.
~/.bash_logout
This is read when a login shell exits, not when it starts.
~/.bash_profile
Right. Bash reads this per-user file next (or ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile if it does not exist).
/etc/profile
Right. This system-wide file is read first by login shells.

q.q: A file `users.txt` has lines such as `alice:x:1001:1001::/home/alice:/bin/bash`. Which command prints only the login shell field of every line?
o: cut -d: -f7 users.txt
Right. -d sets the delimiter to a colon and -f7 picks the seventh field, which is the shell here.
cut -f7 users.txt
The default delimiter of cut is a tab, so the colon-separated lines would be printed whole.
cut -c7 users.txt
-c7 prints only the seventh character of each line, not a field.
sort -t: -k7 users.txt
This sorts the lines by field seven but still prints all fields.

q.q: You need the list of unique values of a file, each with the number of times it appears, most frequent first. Which pipeline does it?
o: uniq -c file | sort -nr
Without sorting first, uniq counts only adjacent duplicates, so the counts would be wrong.
sort -u file | wc -l
This prints only the number of unique lines, not each value with its count.
sort file | uniq -c | sort -nr
Right. uniq only joins neighbors, so sort comes first. -c adds the counts, and the last sort puts big numbers on top.
sort file | uniq -d
This prints only the lines that are repeated, with no counts.

q.q: Which command prints the last 20 lines of /var/log/syslog and keeps showing new lines as they are added?
o: head -n 20 --follow /var/log/syslog
head shows the start of a file, and its -f option is not for following.
tail -n 20 -f /var/log/syslog
Right. -n sets the number of lines and -f follows the file as it grows.
cat -n 20 /var/log/syslog | tail -f
cat -n numbers lines, and 20 would be read as a file name.
less +F -n 20 /var/log/syslog
less has +F to follow, but -n there turns line numbers off. The command does not choose the last 20 lines.

q.q: Which command changes every lowercase letter in the input to uppercase?
o: tr -d a-z
-d deletes the characters in the set instead of changing them.
sed 's/[a-z]/A-Z/'
This replaces the first lowercase letter in a line with the literal text A-Z.
tr a-z A-Z
Right. tr translates characters one by one from the first set to the second set. It reads standard input.
cut -c a-z
cut takes character positions as numbers. It does not change case.

q.q: Which command splits `big.log` into pieces of 100 lines each, with names starting with part_?
o: split -l 100 big.log part_
Right. -l sets lines per piece, and the last argument is the prefix, giving part_aa, part_ab and so on.
split -b 100 big.log part_ --verbose
-b sets the size of each piece in bytes, so you would get pieces of 100 bytes.
csplit -z big.log 100 part_
csplit splits at patterns or line numbers and takes different arguments. It does not use a prefix this way.
cut -l 100 big.log part_
cut has no -l option for pieces.

q.q: What does the command `cp -a /srv/site /backup/` do that plain `cp -r` does not?
o: It moves the files and removes the originals
Moving is done with mv. cp always keeps the originals.
It copies recursively and keeps permissions, owners, times and links
Right. -a is archive mode. It is meant to make the copy as close to the original as possible. Preserving owner needs root.
It compresses the data while copying
cp has no compression option.
It copies only the files that are newer than those in the destination
That is the -u option. -a does not compare dates.

q.q: In a directory you run `ls *.log`, but an extra file named `-rf` exists there. Which problem could this cause when you later type `rm *`, and what is the safe habit?
o: rm refuses to run at all when a file name starts with a dash
rm runs and treats the name as an option, which is the problem.
Nothing happens because * never matches names with a dash
* matches such names. Only names starting with a dot are skipped by default.
The file -rf is a special file that disables wildcards
There is no such special file. Wildcards are handled by the shell.
The shell expands * to include -rf, so rm may see an option. Use `rm -- *` or `rm ./*`
Right. The shell expands the pattern before rm runs. -- ends option processing and ./ makes names start with a path, so names cannot look like options.

q.q: Which command would create the directory tree /srv/app/logs/2026 in one step, even if /srv/app does not exist yet?
o: mkdir /srv/app/logs/2026
Without -p, mkdir fails when a parent directory is missing.
touch -p /srv/app/logs/2026
touch makes files and has no -p option to make directories.
mkdir -r /srv/app/logs/2026
mkdir has no -r option. The option for parents is -p.
mkdir -p /srv/app/logs/2026
Right. -p creates all missing parent directories and gives no error if one already exists.

q.q: Which command lists only the files and directories in the current directory whose names start with `rep`, followed by exactly one character, and then `.txt`?
o: ls rep?.txt
Right. ? stands for exactly one character, so rep1.txt matches but rep10.txt does not.
ls rep*.txt
* stands for any number of characters including none, so rep10.txt would match too.
ls rep+.txt
+ is not a wildcard in shell patterns, so this looks for a file literally named rep+.txt.
ls rep.?.txt
This looks for a literal dot after rep, which is not what was described.

q.q: Which tar command creates a gzip-compressed archive named backup.tar.gz of /etc, showing the files as it works?
o: tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /etc
x extracts. This would try to unpack an archive and not make one.
tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /etc
Right. c creates, z compresses with gzip, v is verbose and f names the archive file.
tar -tzvf backup.tar.gz -C /etc
t lists the contents of an existing archive.
tar -czvf /etc backup.tar.gz
This names /etc as the archive file, so tar errors out.

q.q: You want to check what is inside archive.tar.xz before you unpack it. Which command lists the contents without extracting?
o: tar -xf archive.tar.xz -C /tmp
-x extracts files, here into /tmp, so it changes the disk and does not just list the contents.
tar -rf archive.tar.xz newfile
-r appends files to an archive, which would change it.
tar -tf archive.tar.xz
Right. -t lists. Modern GNU tar detects the compression itself while reading.
xz -d archive.tar.xz
This decompresses the file on disk and replaces it with archive.tar. It does not list anything.

q.q: Which command copies a disk's first 512 bytes (the boot sector) to a file for backup?
o: dd if=mbr.bak of=/dev/sda bs=512 count=1
The input and output are swapped, so this would overwrite the boot sector with a file.
cp /dev/sda mbr.bak
This tries to copy the entire disk, which is huge, not just 512 bytes.
dd if=/dev/sda of=mbr.bak bs=512 count=1
Right. dd reads the input file, writes the output file and, with count=1 and bs=512, copies exactly one block of 512 bytes.
tar -cf mbr.bak /dev/sda1
This archives a partition's device node, not the boot sector, and it is not the right way to copy raw data.

q.q: Which command compresses the file `data.csv` in place, so that only `data.csv.gz` is left?
o: gzip data.csv
Right. gzip replaces the original with a compressed copy and adds .gz.
gzip -c data.csv
-c writes to standard output and leaves the original file in place.
gunzip data.csv
gunzip decompresses and needs a .gz file.
zcat data.csv
zcat prints the uncompressed content of a .gz file and does not compress anything.

q.q: A backup script runs `tar -czf /backup/etc.tgz /etc > /dev/null 2> errors.log`. What ends up in errors.log?
o: Only the normal output (standard output) from tar
Standard output is sent to /dev/null by the first redirect.
Both standard output and standard error
Standard output was thrown away, so only the second stream reaches the file.
Nothing, because tar -c never prints
tar can write errors such as permission denied, and these go to standard error.
Only the error messages (standard error) from tar
Right. 2> sends file descriptor 2, standard error, to the file. Standard output goes to /dev/null.

q.q: Which command line saves both the normal output and the errors of `make` into one file called build.log?
o: make 2>&1 > build.log
Here stderr is copied to the terminal first, and only afterward stdout is sent to the file, so errors still go to the screen.
make > build.log 2>&1
Right. The first redirect points stdout at the file, and 2>&1 then points stderr to wherever stdout goes.
make > build.log 1>&2
This sends stdout to the stderr stream, which is the terminal, so the file would not get both.
make >& build.log 2
The trailing 2 is passed to make as an argument and is not a redirect.

q.q: Which command shows the output of `dmesg` on screen and at the same time saves it to a file called boot.txt?
o: dmesg > boot.txt
This sends all output to the file, so nothing appears on screen.
dmesg | cat > boot.txt
This only passes the data to a redirect, so nothing is shown on screen.
dmesg < boot.txt
< reads input from a file. It does not save output.
dmesg | tee boot.txt
Right. tee copies standard input to standard output and to each named file.

q.q: You want to find all `.tmp` files under /var/tmp and delete them, even if some names contain spaces. Which command is the safest?
o: find /var/tmp -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 rm
Right. -print0 and -0 separate names with a null character, so spaces and newlines in names cannot split a name.
find /var/tmp -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm
xargs splits on whitespace, so a name like my file.tmp would be passed as two names.
rm $(find /var/tmp -name '*.tmp' -type f)
The shell splits the output on spaces, which breaks names with spaces.
ls /var/tmp | grep tmp | rm
rm does not read file names from standard input.

q.q: What does `cat <<EOF > note.txt` followed by three lines and a line with only EOF do?
o: It reads note.txt and stops when it finds the word EOF in it
< is for reading from a file. <<EOF reads from the following lines.
It writes the three typed lines into note.txt
Right. This is a here document. The shell feeds the text up to the closing marker to cat as input.
It appends the lines to note.txt
Appending needs >>. A single > replaces the file.
It deletes note.txt if it contains the word EOF
No data is tested or deleted. The marker only closes the here document.

q.q: What is true about the command `sort data | tee sorted.txt | uniq -c`?
o: sorted.txt gets the counts that uniq -c prints
tee sits before uniq in the pipe, so it only sees what sort wrote.
uniq -c reads data straight from sort, and tee only shows it on the screen
In a pipe, tee's standard output is what feeds uniq. Nothing bypasses tee.
sorted.txt gets the sorted lines, and uniq -c counts those same lines
Right. tee copies what it reads to the file and also passes it on unchanged, so the file holds the output of sort and uniq reads the same data.
tee ends the pipe, so uniq -c gets no input
tee writes to standard output as well as to the file, so the pipe continues.

q.q: Which pipeline shows the five biggest items directly inside /var/log, largest first?
o: du -s /var/log/* | sort | head -5 | tac
A plain sort orders as text and ascending, so the list would not start with the biggest.
du -s /var/log | sort -nr | head -5
Without the *, du -s prints a single total for /var/log, so there is nothing to rank.
ls /var/log | head -5
This shows five names in alphabetical order, not sizes.
du -s /var/log/* | sort -nr | head -5
Right. du -s gives one total per item matched by the *, sort -nr orders the numbers high to low, and head keeps five lines.

q.q: A user types `command1 && command2 || command3`. Command1 succeeds and command2 fails. Which commands are run in total?
o: command1 and command2 only
|| runs command3 because the left side failed, so it is run too.
command1, command2 and command3
Right. && runs the second command after a success. When command2 fails, || runs command3.
command1 only
command1 succeeded, so && continues with command2.
command1 and command3 only, then it stops
command2 did run and failed, so || then ran command3. Command2 is not skipped.

q.q: Which command reads names from standard input and runs `ls -ld` on up to 10 names at a time?
o: xargs -n 10 ls -ld
Right. -n sets the maximum number of arguments that xargs gives to one run of the command.
xargs -P 10 -n 1 ls -ld
-P sets how many commands run in parallel, not how many names each gets.
tee -n 10 ls -ld --append
tee copies streams and does not run commands from names.
exec -n 10 ls -ld
exec is a bash builtin that replaces the shell, and it has no such option.

q.q: You start a long job with `sleep 600` and then press Ctrl+Z. What happened?
o: The job was killed and its output is lost
Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, which usually ends a program. Ctrl+Z only pauses.
The job keeps running in the background and the shell is released
This would be the effect of starting with & or using bg after the stop. Ctrl+Z alone pauses it.
The job is suspended; resume it with bg or fg
Right. Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, which pauses the process. bg continues it in the background and fg returns it to the foreground.
The job moved to another terminal
Jobs belong to the shell that started them and are not moved.

q.q: A script started from an SSH session must keep running after you log out. You did not start it with any special tool. Which approach would have kept it alive?
o: nohup ./script.sh &
Right. nohup makes the process ignore the hangup signal that is sent when the terminal closes, and & puts it in the background.
./script.sh 2>&1 | tee out.log
tee only copies the output to a file. The job stays tied to the terminal and is still hit by the hangup signal when it closes.
./script.sh | less
less is a pager that needs the terminal. It does not detach anything.
fg ./script.sh
fg brings a job to the foreground, which ties it to the terminal.

q.q: Which signal can a process catch or ignore, and is the normal way to ask it to end cleanly?
o: SIGKILL (9)
SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored. The kernel ends the process at once, with no cleanup.
SIGSTOP (19)
SIGSTOP cannot be caught either, and it pauses a process instead of ending it.
SIGSEGV (11)
The kernel sends this when a program accesses bad memory. It is not used to ask for a clean exit.
SIGTERM (15)
Right. kill sends SIGTERM by default. A well-written program catches it, saves its data and exits.

q.q: A process with PID 4120 is stuck in an uninterruptible state D and does not react to `kill -9`. What does this most likely mean?
o: It is a zombie, so its parent has to be killed first
Zombies show state Z, not D, and they use no CPU or memory.
It waits in the kernel for I/O, such as a hung disk or NFS server
Right. A process in D state sleeps inside the kernel. Signals are delivered only when it comes back to user mode.
It is stopped by Ctrl+Z and needs fg
A stopped job shows state T, and SIGKILL still works on it.
It is running with a niceness of 19 so it ignores signals
Niceness affects scheduling and not signals.

q.q: Which command finds the PIDs of all processes whose command name contains `httpd` and prints them one per line?
o: pidof -l httpd
-l is not a pidof option, and pidof matches an exact name only.
pstree httpd
pstree draws a tree for the given PID or user and does not search for a name.
pgrep httpd
Right. pgrep matches process names and prints PIDs, so you do not need to parse ps output.
kill -l httpd
kill -l lists signal names.

q.q: You need to end every process called `firefox` that belongs to the current user without looking up PIDs. Which command does it?
o: kill firefox
kill needs a PID or job number, not a name.
killall -9 -u root firefox
This selects root's processes, not the current user's, and -9 skips a clean exit.
skill firefox -l
-l is not a valid use here and the form is wrong.
pkill -u $USER firefox
Right. pkill matches by name and sends SIGTERM. -u limits the match to the owner's processes.

q.q: In `top`, what does a load average of `4.00 3.80 3.50` on a 4-core machine tell you?
o: The system has used 400 percent of its memory
Load average is not a memory figure.
About 4 tasks were running or waiting on average, so all 4 cores are about busy
Right. Load average counts tasks that run or wait for CPU or uninterruptible I/O. On 4 cores, 4.0 means all cores are about busy.
Four users are logged in at this time of day
Users are shown elsewhere. The load average does not count them.
The machine has been up for 4 days
Uptime is displayed separately.

q.q: Which command runs a persistent terminal session that you can detach from and later reattach to, after an SSH connection drops?
o: tmux or screen
Right. These multiplexers keep the session running on the server. You reconnect and attach to it again.
watch -n 5
watch repeats a command on an interval. It does not keep a session.
nice
nice sets the priority of a new process.
jobs
jobs lists background jobs of the current shell, which are lost when the shell ends.

q.q: Which TWO signals cannot be caught, blocked or ignored by a process? (Choose two.)
o: SIGINT
A program can catch this. It is what Ctrl+C sends.
SIGKILL
Right. The kernel ends the process at once without giving it a chance to clean up.
SIGTERM
A program can catch this and exit cleanly, or ignore it.
SIGSTOP
Right. The kernel pauses the process, and the process cannot intercept it.
SIGHUP
A program can catch this and, for example, reload its configuration.

q.q: A batch job must run with lower priority so it will not slow down interactive users. Which command starts it correctly with the lowest priority a normal user can set?
o: nice -n -19 ./job.sh
A negative value raises the priority, and only root may do that.
renice 19 ./job.sh
renice changes the priority of a process that already runs and needs a PID, not a script name.
nice -n 19 ./job.sh
Right. A higher nice value means a lower priority. 19 is the lowest priority.
nice --priority=high ./job.sh
This is not a valid option for nice, and high is not a value.

q.q: Process 3301 belongs to you, and you are a normal user with no special limits. You run `renice -n -3 -p 3301`. What happens?
o: It works, because you are the owner of the process
Ownership lets you make it nicer. Raising its priority is a privileged action.
It is refused, because only root may lower a nice value
Right. Normal users can make their own processes nicer (a higher number) but cannot raise priority again.
It kills the process and restarts it with a better priority
renice never restarts a process. It only changes the value of a running one.
It changes the process to the real-time scheduling class
renice changes only the nice value, not the class.

q.q: As root, you want to give an already running process with PID 812 a higher priority than normal. Which command does it?
o: renice -n -5 -p 812
Right. A negative value raises priority, and only root may set it. -p names the PID.
nice -n -5 812
nice starts new commands. It does not change the priority of a running PID.
renice -n 5 -p 812 --user
A positive value lowers the priority, which is the opposite of what is needed.
kill -SIGPRIO 812
There is no such signal.

q.q: Which grep command prints the lines in /etc/passwd that start with `root`?
o: grep 'root$' /etc/passwd | head
$ anchors the match to the end of the line, so this finds lines ending in root.
grep -v root /etc/passwd
-v inverts the match and shows all lines without root.
grep '^root' /etc/passwd
Right. ^ anchors the match to the start of the line.
grep -c root /etc/passwd --color
-c prints only a count of matching lines, not the lines.

q.q: With basic regular expressions in grep, which pattern matches the three-digit number lines such as 404 and 503, but not 4040?
o: grep '[0-9]\{3\}' file
Without -x or anchors, 4040 contains three digits in a row and would match.
grep '[0-9]{3}' file
In basic regular expressions { } are literal characters, so this looks for the text with braces.
grep '[0-9]*3' file
This matches any line with a 3 that follows zero or more digits, which is very broad.
grep -x '[0-9]\{3\}' file
Right. -x requires the whole line to match, and \{3\} repeats the digit class exactly three times.

q.q: In an extended regular expression, what does `colou?r` match?
o: Only colour
The u is optional, so color matches as well.
color, colour and colouur
? allows zero or one u. It does not allow two.
Both color and colour
Right. ? makes the previous character optional, so the u may be there or not.
Only a literal question mark after colou
? is a special character in extended expressions and is not a literal one.

q.q: Which command replaces every occurrence of `http` with `https` in the file urls.txt and writes the change back into the same file?
o: sed 's/http/https/g' urls.txt
Without -i, sed prints the result to the screen and the file is not changed.
sed -n 's/http/https/' urls.txt
-n hides normal output, and without g or -i, nothing would be changed in the file.
grep -i 's/http/https/g' urls.txt
grep searches and does not substitute.
sed -i 's/http/https/g' urls.txt
Right. -i edits the file in place, and the g flag replaces all matches on each line.

q.q: Which egrep (or grep -E) pattern matches lines that contain either `error` or `fail`?
o: grep 'error|fail' log
In basic expressions the | is a literal character, so the line would need the text error|fail.
grep -E 'error|fail' log
Right. In extended regular expressions | means or.
grep -E 'error&fail' log
& has no special meaning here, so it would look for that literal text.
grep -F 'error|fail' log
-F treats the pattern as a fixed string, so | is literal again.

q.q: Which sed command prints only lines 5 to 8 of a file?
o: sed -n '5,8p' file
Right. -n turns off the default printing, and 5,8p prints only that range.
sed '5,8p' file | sort -u
Without -n, every line is printed once, and lines 5 to 8 are printed twice.
sed '5,8d' file | cat -n
d deletes the lines in that range and prints all the others.
sed -n '5-8p' file
The range separator is a comma. A dash is not valid.

q.q: In vi, which ex command deletes every line of the file that starts with `#`?
o: v is the opposite of g: it acts on lines that do NOT match, so this would delete everything except the comments.
This only removes the # character from the current line. The lines stay.
The d command takes no pattern here, so this is not valid and deletes nothing useful.
Right. g runs the command on every line that matches the pattern. ^# anchors # to the start of the line, and d deletes it.

q.q: You edited a file in vi and want to leave and throw away your changes. Which command does that?
o: Press Esc, then type :q! and press Enter
Right. The ! forces the quit and discards changes since the last save.
Press Esc, then type :wq and press Enter to save and quit
This writes the changes and then quits, which keeps them.
Press Esc, then type :q and press Enter to close vi
vi refuses to quit when there are unsaved changes and shows an error.
Press Ctrl+Z
This suspends vi in the background, and the changes are not lost.

q.q: In vi, which command, typed in command mode, replaces every `foo` with `bar` in the whole file without asking for confirmation?
o: `:s/foo/bar/`
This changes only the first match on the current line.
`:%s/foo/bar/g`
Right. % means all lines and g means all matches on each line.
`:%s/foo/bar/`
Without g, only the first match on each line is changed.
`/foo/bar/g` then Enter
The slash starts a search, and it does not replace text.

q.q: In vi, you are in command mode with the cursor in the middle of a line. Which key deletes from the cursor to the end of the line and then switches to insert mode?
o: D
Capital D also deletes to the end of the line, but you stay in command mode.
cc
cc changes the whole line, so the text before the cursor is deleted too.
C
Right. Capital C changes the rest of the line: it deletes from the cursor to the end and starts insert mode.
x
x deletes only the one character under the cursor and stays in command mode.

q.q: Which choice is true of GNU nano compared with vi?
o: It is modeless: you type at once, and commands are shown at the bottom
Right. Nano has no separate insert and command modes, so beginners can edit right away.
It has separate insert and command modes like vi
That describes vi. Nano does not use modes.
It cannot edit system configuration files at all
Nano can edit any file that the user may write. It is often used for config files.
It can only be used through a graphical desktop
Nano runs in a text terminal.

q.q: You must create a partition on a 6 TB disk. Which statement is correct about the partition table type?
o: GPT cannot be used on a disk bigger than 2 TB
GPT was designed to remove that limit.
MBR supports an unlimited number of primary partitions on a disk
MBR allows only four primary partitions, and one of them may be an extended partition.
MBR cannot address beyond 2 TiB, so GPT is needed for the whole disk
Right. MBR stores sector numbers in 32 bits, which caps addressable space at 2 TiB. GPT uses 64-bit values.
Only UEFI systems can read a GPT disk of any kind
Linux can use GPT disks on BIOS systems too, with a BIOS boot partition for GRUB.

q.q: Which command creates an ext4 filesystem on the partition /dev/sdb1 and sets its label to DATA?
o: mkfs -t xfs -L DATA /dev/sdb1
This would make an XFS filesystem, not ext4.
mkfs.ext4 -L DATA /dev/sdb1
Right. mkfs.ext4 builds the filesystem, and -L sets the label.
mke2fs -n -L DATA /dev/sdb1
-n makes mke2fs only pretend (a dry run), so no filesystem is created.
fdisk -L DATA /dev/sdb1
fdisk handles partition tables, and it has no option to build a filesystem.

q.q: You created a partition /dev/sdb2 for swap. Which pair of commands prepares it and turns it on right away?
o: mkfs.swap /dev/sdb2 then mount /dev/sdb2
There is no mkfs.swap for this purpose, and swap is not mounted in a directory.
swapon /dev/sdb2 then mkswap /dev/sdb2
Swap must be prepared before it can be enabled, and formatting an active swap area would fail.
mkswap /dev/sdb2 then mount -t swap /dev/sdb2 /swap
Swap spaces are enabled with swapon and are not mounted on a directory.
mkswap /dev/sdb2 then swapon /dev/sdb2
Right. mkswap writes the swap signature, and swapon starts using the area. Add an /etc/fstab line to keep it after a reboot.

q.q: Which tool is the best choice to create a partition table and partitions on a disk that uses GPT and gives the ability to script it non-interactively?
o: mkfs.ext4
mkfs makes filesystems. It cannot create partitions.
e2label -v
e2label changes the label of an ext filesystem.
parted
Right. parted supports GPT and MBR and can run commands from the command line, for example parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt.
hdparm
hdparm sets drive parameters, such as power and speed. It does not partition.

q.q: A non-root volume with ext4 on /dev/sdc1 shows errors after a power failure. Which sequence is the safe way to check and repair it?
o: Run fsck on /dev/sdc1 while it is mounted and in use
Checking a mounted writable filesystem can corrupt it.
Run mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc1 to refresh it
mkfs creates a new filesystem, and destroys the old content.
Run tune2fs -O ^has_journal /dev/sdc1 to repair
This removes the journal. It does not repair damage.
umount /dev/sdc1, then run e2fsck -f /dev/sdc1
Right. Repairing a filesystem that is mounted read-write can damage it, so unmount first. -f forces a full check even if the filesystem looks clean.

q.q: Which command displays the superblock information of an ext4 filesystem, such as its block size, inode count and mount count?
o: xfs_info /dev/sdb1
xfs_info is for XFS filesystems.
dumpe2fs -h /dev/sdb1
Right. -h prints only the superblock header details. Without it, the group descriptors are listed too.
blkid /dev/sdb1
blkid shows the UUID, label and type but not block or inode counts.
lsblk -f /dev/sdb1 --output UUID
This shows filesystem type, label, UUID and mount point only.

q.q: An XFS filesystem is damaged. Which command repairs it, and in which state must the filesystem be?
o: xfs_repair, on an unmounted filesystem
Right. xfs_repair works only on unmounted filesystems and does not use fsck-style journal replay. Mount and unmount once first to replay the log.
xfs_check -r, on a mounted and active filesystem
xfs_check only reads and is removed in new versions, and a mounted filesystem should not be repaired.
e2fsck -p, on a mounted filesystem
e2fsck is for ext2, ext3 and ext4, not for XFS.
fsck.vfat, on a mounted filesystem
This is for FAT filesystems.

q.q: You see `No space left on device` when creating a small file, yet `df -h` shows 40% of the space free. What should you check next?
o: swapon -s, because the swap area is full
Swap is not used to store files.
uptime, because high load blocks file creation
Load does not cause this error.
lsmod, because a module was unloaded
Loaded modules are not related to free inodes.
df -i, as the filesystem may be out of inodes
Right. Each file needs an inode. A filesystem full of tiny files can use all inodes while plenty of blocks are free.

q.q: A line in /etc/fstab uses `UUID=1b2c...` instead of /dev/sdb1. What is the main benefit?
o: The mount survives device name changes, because the UUID belongs to the filesystem
Right. Device names such as sdb can change between boots. A UUID stays the same until the filesystem is re-created.
The filesystem is encrypted
A UUID is an identifier only and has no encryption.
The mount is faster
Mount speed is not different.
It stops fsck from ever checking the filesystem
fsck still runs, according to the sixth field.

q.q: What do the last two numbers in `/dev/sdb1 /data ext4 defaults 0 2` mean?
o: 0 is the number of retries and 2 is the timeout in seconds
These are not retry or timeout values.
0 is the mount order and 2 is the user ID
Mount order follows the file order, and the user ID is not in these fields.
0 means no dump backup, and 2 means fsck checks it after root
Right. The fifth field is for the dump tool, and the sixth sets the check order: 1 for root, 2 for others, and 0 for no check.
0 means read-only and 2 means read-write
Read-only or read-write is controlled by the options field.

q.q: Which command shows which processes are using a filesystem mounted at /mnt/usb, so you can find out why `umount /mnt/usb` says target is busy?
o: mount -l /mnt/usb --show-labels
mount -l lists mounts. It does not list processes.
lsof /mnt/usb or fuser -vm /mnt/usb
Right. Both list processes that have files open on that mount, or that have it as a working directory.
lsblk /mnt/usb --tree
lsblk lists block devices, not the processes using them.
blkid /mnt/usb
blkid reads filesystem identifiers from devices.

q.q: You want a data disk mounted read-only with no ability to run programs or interpret setuid bits from it. Which set of mount options does this?
o: rw,noexec,nosuid,relatime
rw allows writes, so the disk is not read-only.
ro,exec,suid
exec and suid are the default permissive settings and allow what you want to prevent.
ro,noexec,nosuid
Right. ro blocks writes, noexec stops execution of binaries, and nosuid ignores setuid and setgid bits.
ro,noatime,nodev,relatime
noatime and nodev do not block execution or setuid bits.

q.q: A USB stick with a FAT filesystem is mounted at /mnt/usb. FAT stores no Unix owners, and the files there must belong to the user with uid 1000. Which mount options set that owner?
o: chown=1000
chown is a command and not a mount option.
Right. FAT has no Unix owners on disk, so the mount options decide who owns every file that appears.
owner=all,group=all
This is not a valid option for FAT.
user=1000
The user option lets normal users mount the device. It does not set the owner of the files.

q.q: A systemd system has `/mnt/data` mounted by a .mount unit. Which rule applies to the unit file name?
o: It can be any name, as long as it ends in .mount
If the name does not match the Where= path, systemd refuses the unit.
It must be data.mount
The whole path has to be included, with the leading slash removed.
It must be /mnt/data.mount
Slashes are not allowed in the unit names.
Turn the path's slashes into dashes: mnt-data.mount
Right. systemd requires the unit name to match the mount point path in this escaped form.

q.q: Which command prints the size of each directory directly under /var, stays on the filesystem of /var, uses units like 1.2G, and lists the biggest first?
o: du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -rh
Right. -x does not cross into other mounted filesystems, --max-depth=1 gives one line per child, and sort -rh orders human-readable sizes from the largest down.
du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -rh
Without -x, du also counts filesystems mounted below /var, so the totals can be too big.
du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -n
Plain -n compares only the leading number, so 900K sorts above 2G. It also puts the smallest first.
df -h /var | sort -rh
df shows one line for the whole filesystem and does not give one size per directory.

q.q: `df -h` shows /var at 100%, yet `du -sh /var` adds up to far less. An admin deleted a huge log file an hour ago, and the logging daemon has been running the whole time. What is the most likely reason?
o: The daemon still has the deleted file open, so its blocks are not freed until it closes the file or restarts
Right. A name can be removed while a process holds the file open. df counts the blocks still in use, and du only walks names that still exist.
du -s skips hidden files, so it under-reports
du counts hidden files as well, and -s only sums the totals.
df counts the swap area as part of /var
Swap is separate from /var and df does not add it.
du counts hard links twice, so its total is too small
du counts a hard-linked file once, and double counting would make the total bigger, not smaller.

q.q: A file has permissions `-rwxr-x---` and owner alice and group dev. What can a user bob who is in group dev but is not alice do with it?
o: Read, write and run it
The group does not have write permission.
Read and run it, but not change it
Right. The group part is r-x: read and execute. There is no write bit for the group.
Nothing at all
The group bits give read and execute, and bob is in the group.
Only run it
The group also has read permission.

q.q: The default umask of a user is 022. What permission does a new regular file created by this user get?
o: 755 (rwxr-xr-x)
755 is what a new directory gets with this umask, as directories start from 777.
666 (rw-rw-rw-)
This is the starting value before the umask is applied.
600 would need a umask of 077.
Right. Files start from 666, and the umask 022 removes the write bit for group and others, giving 644 (rw-r--r--).

q.q: Which command sets the SGID bit on a shared directory so new files inside inherit the directory's group, while keeping rwx for owner and group and none for others?
o: chmod 4770 /srv/team -R
The leading 4 sets SUID, which does not affect group inheritance on directories.
chmod 1770 /srv/team -R
The leading 1 is the sticky bit, which stops users from deleting others' files.
chmod 2770 /srv/team
Right. The leading 2 sets SGID, and 770 gives the owner and the group full access, others none.
chmod 770 /srv/team
The SGID bit is not set, so new files take the creator's primary group.

q.q: What does the sticky bit on /tmp (shown as `drwxrwxrwt`) do?
o: It makes every file in the directory executable
The sticky bit does not change execute permission.
It sets the group of new files to the directory's group
That is the work of SGID.
It prevents any file from being created
Everyone may still create files in /tmp.
Only the file owner, directory owner or root may delete or rename files in it
Right. Even though everyone can write to the directory, users cannot remove each other's files.

q.q: The file /usr/bin/passwd shows `-rwsr-xr-x`. What does the letter s mean here?
o: It runs with the rights of its owner (root), not of the caller
Right. The setuid bit lets a normal user change their own password, which needs write access to a protected file.
The file is a symbolic link
A link would show l as the first character.
The file is stored in the swap area
There is no such meaning.
Only the owner may run the file
Others have x as well, and the s does not limit who runs it.

q.q: Which command changes the owner to `www-data` and the group to `web` for /var/www and everything inside it?
o: chown www-data:web /var/www/*
Without -R, only /var/www itself is changed.
chown -R www-data:web /var/www
Right. -R applies the change to the directory and everything inside it. The syntax owner:group sets both.
chgrp -R www-data:web /var/www/*
chgrp takes just a group, so the owner:group form is not valid.
chmod -R www-data:web /var/www
chmod changes permission bits and not the owner.

q.q: Which chmod command in symbolic form gives the group read and write on a file, removes all permissions for others, and leaves the owner's bits alone?
o: chmod 760 file
This sets all bits using numbers and would also change the owner's bits.
chmod g=rw,a-rwx file
a-rwx removes all bits from everyone, including the owner and the group just set.
chmod g+rw,o-rwx file
Right. Symbolic changes add (+) or remove (-) bits for the chosen classes only.
chmod o+rw,g-rwx file
This gives others the bits and removes them from the group, which is the opposite.

q.q: Which statement about hard links is true?
o: A hard link can point to a file on another filesystem
Inode numbers are unique only within one filesystem, so hard links cannot cross filesystems.
A hard link becomes broken when the original name is removed
That happens to symbolic links. A hard link keeps the data.
A hard link has its own separate inode and also holds a copy of the data
It shares the inode, and no data is copied.
A hard link is another name for the same inode, so it survives deleting the first name
Right. The data lasts until the link count falls to zero. Hard links cannot cross filesystems and usually cannot point to directories.

q.q: You run `ln -s /srv/app/current /var/www/site`. Later /srv/app/current is deleted. What happens to /var/www/site?
o: It stays as a dangling symbolic link
Right. A symlink only stores a path. If the target is gone, the link still exists but points to nothing.
It is deleted automatically
The system does not remove symlinks when their target disappears.
It becomes a hard link to the old data
Links do not change type.
It silently points to /srv/app instead
Symlinks never fall back to a parent directory.

q.q: Which command lists every name under /srv that is a hard link to the same inode as /srv/a/report.pdf?
o: find /srv -lname /srv/a/report.pdf
-lname matches symbolic links whose target text is that name. Hard links are not symbolic links.
find /srv -samefile /srv/a/report.pdf
Right. -samefile matches files that have the same inode on the same filesystem, which is what a hard link is.
find /srv -name report.pdf -type l
This lists symbolic links called report.pdf. A hard link may have any name and is a regular file.
find /srv -links 1 -name report.pdf
-links 1 matches files with a single name. A file with hard links has a count above 1.

q.q: Which command creates a symbolic link named `/usr/local/bin/python` pointing to `/usr/bin/python3`?
o: ln -s /usr/local/bin/python /usr/bin/python3
The arguments are reversed. This would create the link in /usr/bin.
ln /usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/python
Without -s, this creates a hard link, not a symbolic link.
ln -s /usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/python
Right. The target comes first and the link name second.
link -s /usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/python
The link command does not take -s.

q.q: Which TWO statements are limits of hard links on a Linux system? (Choose two.)
o: They take as much disk space as the file itself
A hard link adds only a small directory entry, with no copy of the data.
They are normally not allowed for directories
Right. The system blocks them to avoid loops in the directory tree.
They stop working if the original file name is removed
This is true of symbolic links. A hard link keeps the data reachable until its last name is gone.
They cannot point to a file on a different filesystem
Right. A hard link is a name for an inode, and inode numbers are only unique within one filesystem.

q.q: Which command finds all regular files larger than 100 MB under /var that were changed in the last 2 days?
o: find /var -type d -size +100M -mtime +2 -print
-type d means directories, and +2 means older than 2 days.
find /var -type f -size +100M -mtime -2
Right. -type f picks regular files, -size +100M picks files over 100 MiB, and -mtime -2 picks changes in the last 2 days.
find /var -type f -size -100M -mtime -2
-100M means smaller than 100 MiB.
locate /var -size 100M
locate searches a name database and has no -size option.

q.q: You just created a file, and `locate myfile.conf` finds nothing. What is the most likely reason?
o: locate can only find files in /home
locate indexes the whole filesystem except for excluded paths.
The file permissions are 000
locate would still list the file, as the index only needs the names.
The locate database is old. Run updatedb
Right. locate searches a prebuilt index that is usually refreshed once a day, so new files do not show up.
locate needs the -r option to find config files by name
-r is for regular expressions and is not required.

q.q: Which command lists files under / that have the setuid bit OR the setgid bit set?
o: find / -perm /6000
Right. With a slash, find matches when ANY of the listed bits is set, so a file with only setuid or only setgid is shown.
find / -perm -6000
With a dash, find needs ALL the listed bits, so only files with both setuid and setgid would match.
find / -perm 6000
With no prefix, the mode must be exactly 6000, which matches almost nothing real.
find / -perm +6000
The + form was removed from GNU find, and newer versions reject it.

q.q: Which directory should hold a locally compiled program that a system administrator installs, so that it is not overwritten by the package manager?
o: /usr/bin
This is managed by the package manager, which may replace files here.
/bin
/bin holds essential commands and is managed by the distribution.
/proc
/proc is a virtual filesystem and does not store files.
/usr/local
Right. The FHS reserves /usr/local for software installed by the local administrator, and package managers do not touch it.

q.q: Which find command lists files in /home that are owned by user `bob` and have the setuid bit set?
o: find /home -user bob -perm -4000
Right. -user bob matches the owner. -perm -4000 matches files where at least the setuid bit is set.
find /home -user bob -perm 4000 -type f
Without the dash, the permissions must be exactly 4000, which is not a common mode.
find /home -group bob -perm -4000 -type f
-group matches the group, not the owner.
find /home -user bob -perm -2000
2000 is the setgid bit, not setuid.

q.title: Set up a shared team folder with the right permissions
q.scenario: Two designers, ana and raj, need a shared folder at /srv/design on fs01. Right now only root can write there. Make the group designers own it. Then set the mode with ONE chmod command so that the group can read, write and enter it, new files inside keep the group, and everyone else has no access. Do not just open it to everyone.
q.ticket: REQ-3187: new design share on fs01 (Debian 12). Both users are already in the group designers. The folder is empty and owned by root:root with mode 755.
