drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Nov 20 10:12 design

checks.t: Look at the folder's current owner and mode
checks.why: ls -ld shows the folder itself (not what is inside). It starts as drwxr-xr-x root root, so only root can write. Reading the current state first tells you what to change.

checks.t: Make the group designers own the folder
checks.why: chgrp (or chown :group) gives the folder to the group. Group permissions only help the members once the folder belongs to that group.
The group bits start as r-x, so members could enter and read but not create files. The group needs w as well (rwx).

checks.t: Set the setgid bit so new files keep the group
checks.why: With setgid on a directory (the s in rws, or the 2 in 2770), new files get the directory's group, not the creator's own group. Without it, files made by ana would belong to the group ana and raj could not edit them.
The request says everyone else gets no access. Mode 770 or o-rwx leaves others with ---. Keeping r-x for others would let any user read design files.

checks.t: Change the group before the mode
checks.why: The mode only makes sense for the right group. If you set rwx for a group that still is root, the designers get nothing. Fix the owner group first, then set the mode.

checks.t: Check the result with ls -ld after the changes
checks.why: Always confirm. The end state should read drwxrws--- root designers. The s in the group part shows that setgid is set.

checks.t: Did not use mode 777 or open the folder to everyone
checks.why: 777 gives every user on the system full control, including deleting files. The group solves the need, so the extra access is not required and breaks the 'no access for others' rule.

checks.why: top and ps sorted by CPU show ffmpeg (PID 4412, owner chen) at about 395 percent, which means nearly four cores. You need its PID for the next steps.

checks.t: Set the nice value of that process to 10
checks.why: renice changes the priority of a running process by its PID. A higher nice number means a lower priority, so the scheduler gives other work, such as the web server, the CPU first. The job keeps running, just slower when the CPU is busy.
ps -o ni (or ps -l) shows the NI column. Reading it again after renice proves the change took effect.
The manager said the job must finish tonight. Killing it would throw away hours of work. Changing its priority fixes the slow site without losing anything.

checks.t: Did not pick a different nice value than the one requested
checks.why: The ticket asks for exactly 10. Other values change how much CPU the job gets, which the team did not agree to. Follow the request.

q.title: Read the boot log: why did db02 land in emergency mode?
q.scenario: After a planned disk change, db02 no longer boots to the login prompt and shows an emergency shell. Read these lines from `journalctl -b`. Mark every line that records a failure, then say what the log shows.
q.ticket: INC-6155: db02 (Debian 12). The data disk /dev/sdb was re-formatted yesterday. Root and /boot are on other disks.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:41:00 db02 kernel: Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinuz-6.1.0-18-amd64 root=/dev/mapper/vg0-root ro quiet
lines.why: A normal kernel command line. The root filesystem is on LVM and the boot loader found it.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:41:01 db02 kernel: sd 2:0:0:0: [sdb] Attached SCSI disk
lines.why: The kernel found the data disk sdb. The hardware is present, so a missing driver is not the problem.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:41:02 db02 kernel: EXT4-fs (dm-0): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode. Quota mode: none.
lines.why: The root filesystem mounted fine. The root disk is healthy, so a root repair is not needed.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:41:04 db02 systemd[1]: Reached target Swap.

Nov 26 07:42:33 db02 systemd[1]: dev-disk-by\x2duuid-5f3a9c1e\x2d77b0\x2d4d1e\x2d9a52\x2d0c3e1b7d44aa.device: Job dev-disk-by\x2duuid-5f3a9c1e\x2d77b0\x2d4d1e\x2d9a52\x2d0c3e1b7d44aa.device/start timed out.
lines.why: systemd waited 90 seconds for a device with this UUID and gave up. No disk on the system has this UUID any more.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:42:33 db02 systemd[1]: Timed out waiting for device /dev/disk/by-uuid/5f3a9c1e-77b0-4d1e-9a52-0c3e1b7d44aa.
lines.why: The same failure in plain words. Something asked for the UUID, which is what a line in /etc/fstab does.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:42:33 db02 systemd[1]: Dependency failed for /data.
lines.why: The mount for /data could not start because its device never appeared.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:42:33 db02 systemd[1]: Dependency failed for Local File Systems.
lines.why: A required mount failed, so the group of local mounts failed too. Without 'nofail' in fstab, this stops a normal boot.

lines.text: Nov 26 07:42:33 db02 systemd[1]: Reached target Emergency Mode.
lines.why: Because a required mount failed, systemd gives up on a normal boot and drops to emergency mode, where only a root shell is offered.

ask.label: What does this log show?
opts: The /etc/fstab entry for /data uses a UUID that no disk has now, so the mount timed out
The root filesystem is damaged and needs fsck from a rescue disk
The kernel has no driver for sdb, so the disk cannot be used
The default target was changed to emergency.target by an admin
ask.why: The log shows sdb attached and the root mounted fine, but a UUID device timed out and /data failed. After the disk was re-formatted it got a new UUID, and the old one is still in /etc/fstab. Fix: run blkid, put the new UUID in fstab (and consider nofail) and mount -a. The root is not damaged, the driver exists, and the log shows no change of target.

q.title: Re-install GRUB from a rescue disk (BIOS, Debian)
q.scenario: After an admin overwrote the first sector of /dev/sda, the BIOS machine says 'no bootable device'. You booted a rescue disk and have a root shell. The Debian root, with /boot on it, is the logical volume /dev/vg0/root, and the volume group vg0 is already active. Build the steps that bring the boot loader back. Put the needed steps in order and leave out the harmful ones.
q.ticket: INC-6170: srv07 (Debian 12, BIOS, one disk /dev/sda). The data on the disk must not be touched.

rules.why: The installed system's files must be reachable. Mounting the root volume gives you its grub tools and configuration.

rules.text: for d in dev proc sys; do mount --bind /$d /mnt/$d; done
rules.why: grub-install and update-grub look at /dev, /proc and /sys to see the disks. Binding the rescue system's copies into the mounted root lets them work after chroot.
After chroot the shell sees the installed system as its root, so the commands use the installed system's own GRUB files.
This writes the GRUB boot code to the start of the whole disk (not to a partition) so the BIOS can find a loader again.
This rebuilds /boot/grub/grub.cfg so the menu lists the installed kernels.
Leave the chroot, unmount the root and the bind mounts below it cleanly, and reboot into the repaired system.
mkfs creates a new empty filesystem and destroys all the data on the root volume. The data must not be touched.
This writes zeros over the first sector, which holds the boot code and the partition table. It would make the disk worse.
On a BIOS system the loader belongs in the start of the disk, not in a partition. A loader in a partition is not found by the BIOS here.

before.why: The bind mounts go inside /mnt, so the root must be mounted before them.
update-grub must run inside the chroot so it reads the installed system's kernels and /etc/default/grub, not those of the rescue disk.
The bind mounts must be in place before you enter the chroot, because the tools need /dev, /proc and /sys once you are inside.
grub-install must run inside the installed system so it uses that system's GRUB files and config.

last.why: Leaving the chroot, unmounting and rebooting is the final step, because nothing after it would run in this session.

q.title: Place the stages of a Secure Boot UEFI Linux start in order
q.scenario: A server with UEFI Secure Boot and systemd starts up. Place the stages in the order in which they run, from power on to the default target. Three stages do not belong in this boot.

devs.name: UEFI firmware (self-test)
devs.why: The firmware runs first. It tests the hardware and reads the boot entries stored in NVRAM.

devs.name: shim (signed by Microsoft)
devs.why: With Secure Boot, the firmware starts the signed shim first. It checks that the next program is trusted.

devs.name: GRUB from the ESP
devs.why: shim starts GRUB from the EFI System Partition. GRUB shows the menu and loads the kernel and the initramfs into memory.

devs.name: Kernel starts and unpacks initramfs
devs.why: The kernel sets up memory and the CPUs, then unpacks the initramfs and runs its /init program.

devs.name: initramfs finds the real root
devs.why: Early userspace loads drivers, can unlock disks or assemble LVM, and mounts the real root filesystem.

devs.name: Switch root to the real root
devs.why: The initramfs moves to the real root filesystem and starts the init program found there.

devs.name: systemd runs as PID 1
devs.why: The first process on the real root is systemd. It starts the other services.

devs.name: default.target is reached
devs.why: systemd works toward the default target. When it is reached, the services are running and users can log in.

devs.name: MBR boot sector code
devs.why: Legacy BIOS reads boot code from the MBR. A UEFI machine uses the ESP instead.

devs.name: Login prompt
devs.why: The login prompt is started by a service once the target is up. It is a result of the boot, not a stage of it.

devs.name: Manual fsck of /home
devs.why: A check of a filesystem is run by a systemd unit if it is needed. It is not a fixed stage of every boot.
